Then, in the terminal app you already use: astrum You are in your own shell, with your own prompt and colors, plus a bar along the top and one along the bottom. The first tab starts in the directory you ran astrum from. Until you choose a theme, Astrum draws everything in your terminal's own colors, so nothing about how your terminal looks changes. Everything in Astrum can be done with the mouse. The keys are there for people who want them, and the menus show them beside each entry.

The first time you start Astrum, it shows a short walkthrough of four cards: what Astrum is, tabs and panes, the agent, and coming back. Do this With the mouse With the keyboard Next card click Next → or Enter Card before click Back ← Put it away click Skip (or Done on the last card) Esc If you have not chosen a model yet, the card about the agent has a Choose a model button: it closes the walkthrough and opens the list of models your providers offer. The walkthrough is shown once. To see it again, click ≡ menu → Settings → Show the walkthrough. The first card of the walkthrough

The tab bar Along the top is one entry for each tab: its number, its name, and a ✕ that closes it. After the last tab, + opens a new one. If you are in a named session, its name is at the right-hand end. A tab names itself after what it is doing: the program running in it, or else the directory its shell is in. A small mark before the name tells you about a tab you are not looking at, such as an agent at work or a command that has finished. Tabs and panes lists them. The status bar Along the bottom, from left to right: The SHELL chip says your typing goes to the shell. Click it and it turns into ✦ AGENT : your typing now goes to the agent. Click it again to go back. The directory the shell is in. Offers that fit the moment: explain and fix after a command fails, watch while a command of yours is running, take the agent in while ssh or sudo -s has the pane. The model the agent uses, ◆ choose model until you have picked one. Click it for the list. How much the agent may do by itself. It starts at ask first ; click to step through the levels. ? help , a screen with every key. ≡ menu , everything Astrum does, each entry with the key that does the same. Every tab, chip and button on the two bars can be clicked. Keys are shown the way terminals write them: ^B means Ctrl+B .

Click + in the tab bar. A new tab opens, in the same directory as the one you were in. Click a tab to go to it, or turn the mouse wheel over the tab bar to step through them. Drag a tab along the bar to move it, and click its ✕ to close it. The keys: Ctrl+B c for a new tab, Ctrl+B n and Ctrl+B p for the next and previous one, Ctrl+B and a number to go straight to that tab. To give a tab a name of your own, right-click it and choose Rename.

Right-click anywhere in the shell and choose Split right. The pane is divided in two, with a new shell on the right, in the same directory. Split down puts the new one below instead. Click a pane to type in it. Drag the line between two panes to give one more room. Right-click a pane and choose Zoom to let it fill the tab for a while; Unzoom brings the others back. Right-click and choose Close pane when you are done with it, or type exit in its shell. The keys: Ctrl+B | splits side by side, Ctrl+B - one above the other, and Ctrl+B with an arrow key moves between panes. Tabs and panes has the rest.

Click the SHELL chip, or press Ctrl+Space . The agent panel opens, below the shell, or beside it on a terminal at least 140 columns wide. The first time, the agent needs a model. Click ◆ choose model on the status bar (or type /model in the panel) and pick one from the list. Ollama running on this machine is found by itself; the hosted providers need an API key. Providers says how to set each one up. Then type a question and press Enter : what is using the most disk space in this directory? The agent reads what is on your screen and works in your own shell. Before it runs a command, it shows it to you and asks: click Yes , Yes, don't ask again this session , Edit first , or No, do something else . The command then runs in the pane, where you can watch it and take over. Esc stops the agent. You do not have to switch to the panel to ask. At the shell prompt, start a line with # and a space: # why did that last command fail The line goes to the agent instead of the shell, and the keyboard stays where it is. The agent covers everything it can do.

Close the terminal window whenever you like. Your shells keep running, and so does whatever is running in them. To leave without closing the window, click ≡ menu → Detach (keep everything running), or press Ctrl+B d . Astrum says the session keeps running and how to return. Later, in any terminal window: astrum Every tab, split, running program and line of scrollback is where you left it. After a restart of the machine, the tabs, their splits, their directories and what they showed come back too, each pane with a fresh shell. Sessions that come back explains what is kept and for how long.

Tabs and panes : splits, scrollback, finding text, copying, links and pictures. The mouse and the keys : every click, every menu, every key, and how to change them. Sessions that come back : named sessions, stopping one, and what returns after a reboot. Tabs on other machines : a tab on a server over your own ssh , whose shells stay there. The agent : what it can do, and how much it may do on its own. Settings : the settings screen and the config file.

Astrum is one file. To install the latest release as ~/.local/bin/astrum , run this in a terminal: $ curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robert-mcdermott/astrum/main/install.sh | sh Copy Then start it: astrum No sudo is needed, and nothing else has to be installed first: Astrum does not depend on any other program when it runs. (A tab on another machine is reached with the ssh you already have.)

In order, it: Works out which file this machine needs, from what uname says about the system and the processor. A shell running under Rosetta on an Apple silicon Mac still gets the Apple silicon build. Downloads that file and the release's SHA256SUMS from GitHub, over HTTPS only. Checks the file's SHA-256 checksum against its line in SHA256SUMS , and stops if they differ. Puts the file in a temporary place beside where it is going, runs it to see that it is Astrum (and, if you asked for a particular version, that version), and only then moves it into place. A download that went wrong never replaces a copy that works. Installing to the default folder, it also puts the manual page in ~/.local/share/man/man1 , where man astrum finds it. It does not use sudo , change your PATH , edit your shell's startup files or start anything. When it is done it prints the command to start Astrum, and a reminder that a session already running keeps the version it was started with (see Upgrading ). It needs sh , curl , uname , awk , grep , mktemp , and sha256sum or shasum , which nearly every macOS and Linux system has. If one is missing, it says which. If ~/.local/bin is not on your PATH The installer says so, and prints the full path to run instead. To be able to type just astrum , add the folder to your PATH in your shell's startup file ( ~/.zshrc , ~/.bashrc , or ~/.config/fish/config.fish ). For zsh and bash: export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" Open a new terminal afterwards for it to take

System The release file macOS on Apple silicon astrum-darwin-arm64 Linux on x86-64 astrum-linux-amd64 Linux on ARM64 astrum-linux-arm64 The Linux builds are fully static: they need nothing from the system, and run on old and new distributions alike. Release builds exist from version 0.4.0 on. There is no release build for an Intel Mac, or for other systems; the installer says so and stops. An Intel Mac can build from source . Windows There is no Windows build: Astrum is made for Unix-like systems, from how it keeps sessions running to the shells it works with. On Windows 10 and 11 it can run inside WSL2, the Windows Subsystem for Linux, where it is on Linux like anywhere else: In PowerShell, install a Linux distribution: wsl --install (Ubuntu, unless you name another). Open that distribution in Windows Terminal, and use the one-line install there. Run astrum . Your shells are the distribution's, and so are the files the agent works with; your Windows drives are under /mnt/c and so on. Astrum under WSL2 has not been tried yet. What we expect to work differently there: Copying is always sent to the terminal (as OSC 52), which Windows Terminal is meant to put on the Windows clipboard. If it does not, ASTRUM_CLIPBOARD_TOOL=clip.exe set before starting astrum hands the text to Windows' own clip.exe as well, which may garble letters outside plain ASCII. Links are opened with xdg-open , which in WSL often has no browser to open. Set ASTRUM_OPEN_TOOL=wslview (from the wslu package) o

The installer is a short shell script. To read it before running it, download it, look through it, then run it: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSLo install-astrum.sh https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robert-mcdermott/astrum/main/install.sh less install-astrum.sh sh install-astrum.sh sh install-astrum.sh --help lists its options.

h: A particular version, or another folder
x: --version installs a particular release, and --install-dir puts it in another folder (an absolute path): sh install-astrum.sh --version v0.4.0 sh install-astrum.sh --install-dir "$HOME/bin" The version can be written v0.4.0 or 0.4.0 . With a version given, the installer also checks that the program it downloaded reports exactly that version. For the one-line form, the environment variables ASTRUM_VERSION and ASTRUM_INSTALL_DIR do the same, set for the sh at the end of the line: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robert-mcdermott/astrum/main/install.sh | ASTRUM_VERSION=v0.4.0 sh ASTRUM_DOWNLOAD_BASE takes the release files from somewhere other than GitHub: an https:// address of a mirror, or file:/// and a folder on this machine that holds the release file and its SHA256SUMS (files you downloaded by hand, say). The checksum is checked just the same. The manual page is only placed when installing to the default folder.

To install without the script, take the file for your machine and SHA256SUMS from the releases page . With curl , for the latest release on a Mac: curl -fsSLO https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/astrum/releases/latest/download/astrum-darwin-arm64 curl -fsSLO https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/astrum/releases/latest/download/SHA256SUMS Work out the file's checksum and compare it with the line for the same file in SHA256SUMS : shasum -a 256 astrum-darwin-arm64 grep astrum-darwin-arm64 SHA256SUMS On Linux, sha256sum does the same, and can check the file against the list in one step: sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS If the two match, make the file executable and put it on your PATH as astrum : chmod +x astrum-darwin-arm64 && mv astrum-darwin-arm64 ~/.local/bin/astrum

astrum completions bash (or zsh , or fish ) prints a completion script, which completes Astrum's commands, their options and the names of your sessions. The first lines of each script say where it goes: Shell Where bash astrum completions bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/astrum zsh astrum completions zsh > ~/.zfunc/_astrum , with fpath=(~/.zfunc $fpath) in ~/.zshrc before compinit runs fish astrum completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/astrum.fish astrum man prints the manual page. The installer already puts it where man astrum finds it when it installs to the default folder; otherwise, write it to a man1 folder that man searches, such as: mkdir -p ~/.local/share/man/man1 && astrum man > ~/.local/share/man/man1/astrum.1 The manual page is also on this site .

Building needs a Rust toolchain, 1.88 or newer, and a C compiler. Get the source and install from it: git clone https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/astrum cd astrum && cargo install --path . --locked That puts astrum in ~/.cargo/bin . --locked builds with the exact dependency versions recorded in Cargo.lock , the ones Astrum is tested with. To build without installing, the binary is then target/release/astrum : cargo build --release --locked If cargo or astrum is "not found" afterwards, ~/.cargo/bin is not on your PATH ; add . "$HOME/.cargo/env" to your shell's startup file.

Run the one-line install again: it installs the newest release over the old one, with the same checks. A session that is already running keeps running the version it was started with. To move it to the new one, stop it and start it again; its tabs come back: astrum kill astrum Do that for each session you have ( astrum ls lists them, and astrum kill --all stops them all). In the meantime the new astrum can still attach to, list and stop a session the older one started. A session run as a login service needs only astrum kill : the service manager starts it again from the same file, which is now the new version. The changelog says what changed in each release, with notes on upgrading from the one before. If you once installed Astrum with cargo install , that copy is in ~/.cargo/bin , and whichever of the two comes first on your PATH is the one that runs. Remove the one you no longer want ( cargo uninstall astrum for the other), or go on upgrading it the way you installed it.

If you stored API keys with /key , remove each from the system's password store with /key name remove in the agent panel while Astrum is still there. Work from a terminal outside Astrum for the rest. If you set up the login service , remove it, or it starts the session again: astrum service uninstall (and astrum service uninstall -s name for each other session that has one). Stop your sessions: astrum kill --all . Add --forget to discard their saved tabs as well. Delete the program: ~/.local/bin/astrum , or wherever you installed it. What is left are your files. Delete them too if you want nothing to remain: What Where Settings, your own rules and skills ~/.config/astrum Saved sessions, conversations, builds kept for other machines ~/.local/share/astrum The manual page ~/.local/share/man/man1/astrum.1 Completion scripts wherever you put them Session sockets and server logs /tmp/astrum-<uid> (your user id) A machine you opened a tab on has its own copy in ~/.local/bin/astrum there, if Astrum put it there.

Each pane remembers the last 10,000 lines its programs printed. scrollback in the config file changes that; the change applies to shells started afterwards. Do this With the mouse With the keyboard Scroll back and forward turn the mouse wheel over the pane Shift+PageUp / Shift+PageDown , or Ctrl+B PageUp / PageDown Back to the bottom scroll down, or start typing any key typed into the shell A full-screen program (an editor, a pager) has the screen to itself. If it uses the mouse, the wheel goes to it; if it does not, the wheel is sent to it as arrow keys, so a pager such as less scrolls with the wheel too.

The search looks through everything a pane still remembers, newest first, and finds as you type. Do this With the mouse With the keyboard Open the search right-click the pane → Find…, or ≡ menu → Find in scrollback Ctrl+B / Next older match click ↑ on the search bar Enter or ↑ Next newer match click ↓ ↓ Close the search click ✕ Esc The matches are lit up in the pane, and the bar says which one you are on and how many there are ( 3 of 12 ), or that there is no match. Small letters find capitals too; a capital letter in what you type makes the search exact. Backspace takes back a letter, Ctrl+U clears the text, and pasting puts the pasted text into the search. Pressing Tab keeps the search and turns it into copy mode : n and N then step to the older and newer matches, v starts selecting, y copies, and q leaves. Click the search text to type in it again. Finding a word in what has scrolled by

With the mouse: Drag across text to select it. When you let go, it is copied, and Astrum says how many characters. Double-click a word to select it, and click a third time for the whole line. Drag past the top or bottom of the pane and it scrolls, so a selection can reach into the scrollback. Click anywhere else to let go of the selection. Copied text is handed to your terminal app's clipboard (that also works over SSH, where the terminal lets programs set the clipboard), and to the clipboard tool of the machine astrum runs on: pbcopy on macOS, wl-copy or xclip on Linux. ASTRUM_CLIPBOARD_TOOL , set before starting astrum , names another program to hand it to, or none to leave copying to the terminal alone. To keep a selection from being copied the moment you let go, turn off ≡ menu → Settings → Copy text as soon as it is selected ( copy_on_select = false in the config file). Paste the way you always do in your terminal app. What you paste goes to wherever the keyboard is: the shell, the agent panel, or a search. In programs that use the mouse Programs such as vim and htop handle the mouse themselves and get your clicks and drags as usual. Hold Shift while you drag to select text inside them with Astrum's selection instead, and hold Shift while you right-click to get Astrum's menu rather than theirs.

Copy mode is the keyboard's way to select text. Press Ctrl+B [ , or click ≡ menu → Select with the keyboard. A COPY chip appears on the bar, and a cursor in the pane that moves through the screen and the scrollback. Nothing typed in copy mode reaches the shell. Key Does arrows, or h j k l move the cursor w / b / e to the next word, the word before, the end of the word W / B / E the same, with words separated only by spaces 0 / $ , or Home / End to the start or end of the line ^ to the first character on the line that is not a space H / M / L to the top, middle or bottom of the pane { / } to the paragraph before or after % to the matching bracket g / G to the oldest or the newest line PageUp / PageDown a page back or forward Ctrl+U / Ctrl+D half a page back or forward v or Space start selecting at the cursor V select whole lines Ctrl+V select a block y or Enter copy the selection and leave / search, as in Finding text n / N the next older or newer match q or Esc leave ( Esc first lets go of a selection, if there is one) A click in the pane moves the cursor there. The ✕ on the bar leaves copy mode, and so does Ctrl+B [ again.

A web address in a pane can be followed, and so can a link a program marked as one ( ls --hyperlink , gh , compilers that link to their documentation). Point at it and the status bar shows where it really goes, which for a marked link may not be what its text says. Right-click it for Open link and Copy link. Or hold Ctrl and click it. Some terminals keep Ctrl -click for themselves (macOS Terminal is one); there, the right-click is the way. Astrum opens web and mail links and nothing else, with the system's own open (macOS) or xdg-open (Linux) on the machine where you ran astrum . A link to a file is not opened, because opening a file can mean running it; it can still be copied. ASTRUM_OPEN_TOOL names another program to open links with, or none .

A picture a program prints is shown in the pane: imgcat , kitten icat , chafa , img2sixel , or a plotting library that draws to the terminal. It scrolls with the text around it, is cleared with it, and is there again when you look back through the scrollback. Programs send pictures in three ways (iTerm2's, kitty's and sixel), and Astrum understands all three. Each attached terminal is sent the picture in a way that terminal has: Your terminal What it is shown iTerm2, WezTerm everything, except raw pixels a program sent compressed in kitty's way Ghostty, kitty pictures sent in kitty's way, and PNG files sent in iTerm2's A terminal that only draws sixel sixel pictures macOS Terminal, and others with no pictures a line saying what the picture is Where a picture cannot be shown, a faint block the size it would have been takes its place, with a line such as PNG 640×480 · this terminal cannot show it . The same block stands in while a picture is partly off the edge of its pane or under a menu: a terminal cannot be asked to draw part of a picture, so it is drawn whole or not at all. A picture is drawn once it has been still for a moment, not at every line while output is pouring past. Things to know: A program finds out whether pictures work by asking, and is answered for the terminal you are using at that moment. The same session can be open in several terminal windows at once: run astrum in another window (with -s name for a named session ). Each window has its own view of the session: its own tab in front, its own menus, drawn edge to edge at its own size. So one window can stay on a build while another edits in a different tab. Two windows looking at the same tab share it: what is typed in one shows in the other. A tab's shells can only have one size, so they are sized for the window that used the tab last. The other window shows the tab at that size, with dots where it does not reach, until a key or a click in that window brings the tab over to its own size. Each window is sent pictures in the way its own terminal can show them. Ctrl+B d detaches the window you are in; Ctrl+B D detaches every window from the session. See Sessions that come back .

The prefix key Most of Astrum's keys come after a prefix key, Ctrl+B unless you change it: press Ctrl+B , let go, then press the key. Ctrl+B c is a new tab. Keys are case-sensitive: Ctrl+B d detaches this window, Ctrl+B D every window. After the prefix, the status bar shows PREFIX and what can follow it, each with its key. They can be clicked as well as typed, so the prefix also works as a way into the menu. They wait ten seconds for you, and moving the pointer starts the wait again. When they do not all fit, ≡ more opens the full menu. Esc , or a key that is none of these, lets go without doing anything. A few things to know: If you are still holding Ctrl when you press the second key, it works all the same: Ctrl+B Ctrl+C is Ctrl+B c , unless you have given that key with Ctrl something of its own. Pressing the prefix twice sends it to the program in the pane, for a program that uses Ctrl+B itself. On screen, keys are written as terminals write them: ^B is Ctrl+B , ^B c is Ctrl+B then c . Keys without the prefix Ctrl+Space switches your typing between the shell and the agent. Shift+PageUp and Shift+PageDown page through the scrollback (unless a full-screen program has the pane). In the agent panel, Esc stops the agent and Shift+Tab steps through how much it may do on its own. The agent has the panel's other keys. Any key you give an action with ctrl or alt in it, as below. The help screen Click ? help on the status bar, or press Ctrl+B ? , for one screen of the keys, grouped

Every key Astrum uses can be changed, in the config file. (The settings screen has the settings most people change; keys are not among them.) astrum config says where the file is, and astrum config --init writes a commented starter file there if there is none. A change takes effect in the running session as soon as you save the file: Astrum says "Settings reloaded", or says what is wrong with the file and changes nothing. Settings has the rest of the file. The prefix and the agent key Two settings at the top of the file: prefix = "ctrl+a" # in place of ctrl+b agent_key = "f2" # in place of ctrl+space On macOS, Ctrl+Space switches input sources when several keyboard layouts are turned on, and some shell plugins use it. If it does something else for you, pick another agent_key , such as "ctrl+backslash" or "f2" . The [keys] table Every other key is in a [keys] table, by the name of what it does: [keys] new_tab = ["c", "ctrl+t"] # Ctrl+B c as before, and Ctrl+T directly next_tab = "alt+right" prev_tab = "alt+left" split_right = "v" detach_all = "none" How it is read: A plain key is pressed after the prefix. A key with ctrl or alt in it works by itself, with no prefix. To put one of those after the prefix instead, write prefix in front: "prefix ctrl+t" . Naming an action replaces all the keys it had. A list gives it several, and "none" (or an empty list) leaves it with none. A key does one thing. Giving it to an action takes it from whatever had it, so two actions can swap keys.

The first time you run astrum , it starts a server in the background for the session. The server owns the shells, runs the agent and draws everything; the astrum in your window only passes your keys and mouse on to it and shows what it is sent back. Closing the window ends only that. The server and your shells carry on, and so does whatever is running in them: a build, a download, an editor you left open, the agent in the middle of a task. Run astrum again, in any terminal window, and you are back where you were: every tab, split, running program and line of scrollback. The same goes for a terminal that goes away by itself: a terminal app that quits, or an SSH connection you ran astrum over that drops when the laptop is closed. While a session runs, Astrum keeps on disk what it would take to rebuild it. It is written about fifteen seconds after anything changes, and once more when the session stops, so a crash loses little. h: Staying up through a logout on Linux
x: Without lingering, systemd stops a user's services at their last logout, and the session stops with them; its tabs come back at the next login. With lingering on, your user's systemd keeps running while you are logged out (and starts when the machine does), so the session stays up: loginctl enable-linger astrum service install and astrum service status both say when lingering is off. loginctl disable-linger turns it off again.

A server started by the service manager does not come from one of your shells, so it has a bare environment. Astrum hands it only what a session needs to find its files and start your shell, as they are in the terminal you run install from: SHELL , LANG , LC_ALL , LC_CTYPE , XDG_CONFIG_HOME , XDG_DATA_HOME , ASTRUM_CONFIG_DIR , ASTRUM_DATA_DIR , ASTRUM_RUNTIME_DIR and ASTRUM_KEYCHAIN_FILE . If none of the language settings is set, it is given a UTF-8 one, so that shells do not garble anything beyond plain ASCII. What that means: API keys set in your shell's startup files do not reach it. Run astrum reload from a shell that has them to pass them in, or store them with /key in the agent panel, which needs nothing in the environment at all. See Providers . A tab on another machine runs ssh with the server's environment, so it does not see your SSH key agent ( SSH_AUTH_SOCK ). Whatever ssh then asks, such as a key's passphrase, is asked in the pane. After changing any of the variables above, run astrum service install again to write them into the service.

astrum service status says whether the service for the session is installed, and whether it is running: Service for session `default`: running /home/me/.config/systemd/user/astrum-default.service or installed, not running , or that no service is installed for the session. On Linux it also says when lingering is off. astrum ls lists the session as usual once it is running. The system's own tools see it too: launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/io.github.robert-mcdermott.astrum.default on macOS, and systemctl --user status astrum-default.service on Linux.

astrum service uninstall removes the service's file, tells the service manager it is gone, and stops the session. Its tabs are kept, and come back the next time you start it with astrum , the ordinary way. Add -s name for another session's service. Run it from a terminal outside that session: stopping the session would cut the command off half-way, so Astrum refuses to run it inside and says why. The file goes before the session is stopped, so even a command that was cut off cannot leave the service to come back at the next login.

With the service installed, astrum kill restarts the session, and astrum kill --forget restarts it empty. To stop it and keep it stopped, remove the service. Closing a session's last shell ends that session for good, as always; the service manager then starts a fresh, empty one, which waits for you to attach. A session under the service is the same session as before: what comes back after a stop or a reboot is decided by restore , just the same.

Level In the config file What it does by itself ask first (the default) autonomy = "ask" Nothing: it asks before every command and every change to a file. auto read-only autonomy = "safe" Runs look-only commands ( ls , cat , git status , git log , df , ps and the like) without asking, and asks for anything that changes things. autopilot autonomy = "auto" Runs commands, changes files, types into programs and uses the tools of MCP servers without asking. It still asks for destructive commands. The level is the session's, and applies to every tab. ask first and auto read-only are remembered for the sessions that follow. Autopilot lasts until the session ends, so that a new session never starts on it by accident; to have it from the start, set autonomy = "auto" under [agent] in the config file. A command counts as look-only when every program on the line is one that only looks ( git log does, git commit does not; find without -delete or -exec ; tail without -f ), and nothing on the line is written to a file with > or run inside $(...) . Allow and deny lists Two lists under [agent] in the config file adjust this for particular commands: [agent] allow = ["cargo test", "git commit", "npm run *test*"] den

The agent changes files with tools of its own, not with an editor, and a change is shown as a diff before anything is written: the lines going out in red, the lines coming in green, with three unchanged lines around each change. The question says what it is: Create a new file, Edit part of one, or Rewrite one whole. A long diff scrolls with the mouse wheel, or with PgUp and PgDn . A change to a file is shown as a diff before anything is written When a change touches several places you can also choose Review each change ( r ) and go through them one at a time: Apply this change ( y ) Skip it ( s ) Cancel the whole edit ( n ) The file is written once you have answered them all, and the agent is told which parts you declined and that it should not make them some other way. If the file changes on disk while the question is open, nothing is written and the agent is told to look again. On autopilot, changes are written without the question. With the agent taken into a shell on another machine there are no file tools: it changes files with commands there, and you approve those as commands (see Other machines ).

What the agent gathers for the model (the output of commands, the files it reads, what is on the terminal, what MCP tools return) is checked for secrets first, and each one is replaced with a note such as [redacted: GitHub token] . Your terminal still shows the real output; only the copy sent to the model changes, and the panel says how many were hidden. It looks for: keys and tokens with a recognizable shape: cloud and source-hosting access keys, API keys, chat and payment service tokens, private key blocks, signed web tokens; passwords in URLs, and credentials in Authorization headers; lines that set something named like a secret ( DB_PASSWORD=... , --api-key=... ), as in an env listing or a .env file; the API keys Astrum itself is using for your providers, the tokens of your MCP servers, and the AWS keys in its environment, anywhere they appear. The agent is told that this happens, and to work with where a secret lives (a file, a variable) rather than with its value. It is deliberately cautious about code, so that token = get_token() stays readable, which means a secret that looks like an ordinary word in an ordinary assignment can get through. Treat it as a safety net, not a guarantee. What you type to the agent yourself is sent as you wrote it. To turn it off, choose ≡ menu → Settings → Hide keys and passwords from the model , or set redact_secrets = false under [agent] .

You do not have to go to the panel to ask something. At the shell prompt, start a line with # and a space: # why is this directory so large Press Enter and the line goes to the agent instead of the shell: it is erased from the prompt, the panel opens to show the agent's work, and the keyboard stays in the shell. If the agent is already busy, the question waits for its next step, like anything typed in the panel. A question typed at the prompt goes to the agent This needs the shell integration (zsh, bash and fish have it), and it applies only to a line you type at a prompt, not to input for a program that is running. Lines such as #!/bin/sh or ## are left alone. To turn it off, choose ≡ menu → Settings → Ask from the shell prompt with "# question" . In the config file, ask_prefix under [agent] chooses another prefix, and ask_prefix = "" turns it off. Astrum works out what you typed from the keys you pressed, including corrections made with Backspace and the arrow keys. For a line the shell had a hand in (recalled from history, or completed with the Tab key) it reads the line from the screen instead, which works when the prompt has not changed since you began typing and nothing follows the cursor. If it cannot be sure, the line goes to the shell as usual. The SHELL chip and Ctrl+Space always work. Plain language With Plain-language lines at the prompt go to the agent turned on in the settings ( natural_language = true under [agent] ), a line that reads as plain language goes to

When a command fails , the status bar shows its exit code ( ✗ exit 1 ) and two offers, explain and fix . Click one, or press Ctrl+B e or Ctrl+B f . The agent is given the command, its exit code and its output. explain has it tell you what went wrong without changing anything; fix has it put the cause right and run the command again to check, asking first as your autonomy level requires. The offer goes away once the agent has seen that failure or you run something else, and it is not made for a command you interrupted yourself with Ctrl+C . /explain and /fix do the same from the panel, and work on the last command even when it succeeded. Both are in ≡ menu as well. While a command of your own is running , the status bar offers watch (or Ctrl+B o , ≡ menu → Watch the running command, or /watch ). The agent then follows that command and tells you how it went when it ends, so you can leave a long build or download and be told the result. /watch then run the tests adds what to do afterwards. It does not interrupt your command, and types into it only when it is plainly waiting for an answer that is safe to give (asked about as usual). Stopping the agent leaves the command running.

h: Adding to a task while it works
x: You can keep typing while the agent works. What you send is held just above the prompt, marked ◷ , and handed to the agent at its next step with the result of whatever it was doing, so you can correct or add to a task without stopping it. Backspace on an empty prompt takes the last waiting message back to change it.

To stop the agent, click in the panel and press Esc (or Ctrl+C ), as the line above the prompt reminds you while it works. A command it started is interrupted too; a command you started yourself, which it was only watching, is left running. Messages still waiting go back to the prompt, and what had not finished is marked in the panel. The conversation stays: ask again and it carries on from there. A turn also stops by itself after 60 steps, each a request to the model and the tools it asked for, and says so. Say "continue" to let it go on.

Each tab has its own conversation, and conversations are saved as they happen, so they outlive the session: after astrum kill , a reboot or a crash, start Astrum again and pick up where you left off. A restored tab opens with the conversation it had; these commands reach the others. /resume reopens the most recent conversation from the directory your shell is in. If there is none from there, it reopens your most recent one from anywhere and says so. /resume words does the same among the conversations whose first prompt contains those words. /conversations lists every saved conversation, newest first, each with its first prompt, how long ago it was used and its directory (or the tab it is open in). Type to filter, click one or press Enter to open it, and press Del twice to delete one. A conversation that is open in a tab cannot be deleted until it is cleared there. /clear starts a new conversation; the old one stays in the list. A resumed conversation continues in the tab's current shell and directory. If it was cut off in the middle of a turn, whatever had not finished is marked as interrupted and the agent is told so. Conversations are stored in ~/.local/share/astrum/conversations/ , one file each, readable only by you. They contain what you asked, what the agent replied and the output of the commands it ran. A conversation that has not been used for 90 days is deleted. To keep nothing on disk, choose ≡ menu → Settings → Keep conversations so they can be resumed . In the con

A model can only take in so much at once, and every request sends the whole conversation again, so a long one gets slow and expensive and in the end does not fit. Compacting fixes that: the model writes a summary of the conversation (what you asked for, what was done, the current state, what comes next) and the summary takes the conversation's place. /compact does it now. /compact keep the exact error messages tells the summary what to take particular care over. It also happens by itself when the conversation reaches 80% of the model's context or 200,000 tokens, whichever comes first, even in the middle of a task, and the agent carries on from the summary. If a provider refuses a request as too long, Astrum compacts and sends it again. When you ask for it with /compact , the summary is shown in the panel so you can see what the agent kept. When it happens by itself, one line says so, and /summary shows the summary whenever you want to read it. Either way, everything above stays in the panel for you to scroll back to; only what is sent to the model changes. Rules files are not part of the conversation and are unaffected. The 200,000-token cap is there because every message sends the whole conversation again, so a model that can take a million tokens gets slow and expensive long before it is full. To leave compacting to you, turn off ≡ menu → Settings → Summarize long conversations when they fill up . In the config file: [agent] auto_compact = true # false: only when you ask wi

The top line of the agent panel shows, for the conversation in that tab, how full the model's context is and how many tokens the conversation has used: sent to the model (in), how much of that the provider served from its prompt cache (cached), received (out), and the total. For example, 12k of 200k context · 85k in · 60k cached · 3k out · 88k total . On a narrow panel it shows as much of that as fits. /usage gives the same breakdown in full, with the model and how many requests there were. The totals are saved with the conversation. Astrum does not turn them into a cost: prices differ by provider and change, so check your provider's own usage page for that.

Type / in the panel for the menu. The commands: Command What it does /model Choose the provider and model; /model provider/name picks one directly. The old one stays saved. /resume Reopen the most recent conversation from this directory; /resume words one whose first prompt has those words. /conversations Browse the saved conversations, to open or delete one. /explain Explain the last command, or why it failed. /fix Work out why the last command failed, and fix it. /watch Follow the command that is running and report when it ends. /compact Summarize the conversation so far to free up context. /summary Show the summary a compacted conversation continues from. /usage The tokens this conversation has used. /copy Copy the agent's last reply to the clipboard. /here Work in the shell this pane has reached: over ssh , in a container, after sudo -s . Out of the box Astrum knows four providers. Each is ready to use once what it needs is there: Provider Kind Where it is Needs ollama OpenAI-compatible http://localhost:11434/v1 Ollama running on this machine openai OpenAI-compatible https://api.openai.com/v1 OPENAI_API_KEY anthropic Anthropic https://api.anthropic.com ANTHROPIC_API_KEY bedrock Amazon Bedrock your AWS region AWS credentials: a Bedrock API key in AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK , or access keys in the environment, or a profile in ~/.aws A local Ollama needs no key (one in OLLAMA_API_KEY is sent if it is set). Any other endpoint that speaks the OpenAI chat API, such as a local model server, a hosted service or a company gateway, can be added in the config file; see Adding a provider . /providers in the agent panel lists what is configured: each provider's kind and address, whether it has a key (for Bedrock, its region and where its credentials come from), and which one is in use.

Click the model name on the status bar ( ◆ and the name, or choose model before there is one). A list opens of the models your providers offer, each with its provider beside it. Type to narrow it, click a model or press Enter to choose it, and press Esc to leave things as they were. The same list is under ≡ menu → Choose a model and ≡ menu → Settings → Model , and behind Ctrl+B m and /model in the panel. Each provider is asked for its models when the list opens, so new models appear without an Astrum update. The list's bottom line names any provider that could not be reached, and why. A hosted OpenAI-compatible provider with no key is not asked. An Anthropic provider without a key shows its usual models, marked "needs an API key". models = [...] in a provider's table adds names to the list, for an endpoint that does not list its models, or one whose list you may not read. To name a model directly, type /model anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5 (the provider, a slash, and the model), or /model and a name alone for a model of the provider in use. The choice is remembered, in this session and the ones after it. It is the session's, not the tab's: every tab's agent uses it from its next request. To set the model in the config file instead: [agent] provider = "anthropic" model = "claude-sonnet-5-5" A choice made inside Astrum takes the place of these until you choose "Forget the choices made here" on the settings screen. The models your providers offer

Each provider is a table under [providers] , and its name is the one you use in /model , /key and provider = : [providers.work] kind = "openai" base_url = "https://llm.example.com/v1" api_key_env = "WORK_LLM_KEY" models = ["my-model"] Setting What it is kind openai for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, anthropic , or bedrock . base_url Where the API is. For an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, requests go to base_url followed by /chat/completions , and the list of models is read from base_url followed by /models . api_key_env The environment variable that holds the API key. api_key The key itself. Simple, but the key then sits in a plain file; see API keys . models Models to offer in the list, beside what the endpoint lists itself. region , profile For Bedrock: see Amazon Bedrock . Saving the config file is enough: a running session takes the change at once, and /model offers the new provider's models. The agent always offers the model its tools, so a model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint needs to support tool calls (function calling). A table named after a built-in provider and of the same kind , such as [providers.ollama] with kind = "openai" , changes only what it sets: an address or key variable it leaves out is the built-in one's. A table of another kind under a built-in's name is yours alone, and needs everything.

A provider's API key can come from three places, used in this order: api_key in the config file. Simple, but the key sits in a plain file. The system's password store, where /key puts it. An environment variable, such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (the one the provider's api_key_env names). Storing a key with /key In the agent panel, /key anthropic asks for the key and shows it as dots while you type or paste it. Enter stores it in the system's password store: the macOS keychain, or on Linux the desktop keyring, through secret-tool (from the package libsecret-tools ). It is used from then on, in every session, with nothing in your shell setup. A key typed this way is kept out of the conversation and out of the prompt's history. /key alone shows where each provider's key is coming from. /key anthropic remove forgets the stored key. /key anthropic followed by the key on the same line stores it too, but the key is shown as you type it. Keys in environment variables A session's background server sees the environment as it was when the session started. If you set or change a key variable afterwards, tell the running session, from the shell that has the new value: astrum reload That passes on the value of each provider's api_key_env variable from that shell, and reads the config file and the stored keys again, so it reports what each provider now uses. Add -s name for a session other than the default. /reload in the panel does the same, except for environment variables. A session run as a l

Create an API key in the Claude Console. In the agent panel, type /key anthropic and paste it. Or set it in the shell you start Astrum from, and put the line in your shell's startup file to keep it for new terminals: export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... Click the model name on the status bar (or type /model ) and choose a model. Models from this provider are labelled anthropic . The model list comes from your account, so new models appear without an Astrum update. On models that support it, the model's reasoning is shown as a running summary on the panel's status line while it thinks. Anthropic's prompt cache is used, which is what the cached figure on the panel counts. For Anthropic's Fable, Opus and Sonnet 5.x models, Astrum opts in to server-side fallback: if a safety classifier declines a request, the API runs it again on another model instead of stopping. To use a different variable name, or a gateway in front of the API: [providers.anthropic] kind = "anthropic" api_key_env = "MY_ANTHROPIC_KEY" # base_url = "https://gateway.example.com"

Bedrock needs AWS credentials and a region. Point Astrum at them in the config file: [providers.bedrock] kind = "bedrock" region = "us-west-2" profile = "my-profile" # a profile from ~/.aws/credentials or ~/.aws/config Then click the model name on the status bar, or type /model . Models from this provider are labelled bedrock . Astrum looks for credentials in this order and uses the first it finds: A Bedrock API key: one stored with /key bedrock , or the variable api_key_env names, which is AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK unless you name another. AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (with AWS_SESSION_TOKEN if set) in the environment. These are skipped when the provider names a profile . An AWS profile: the provider's profile setting, else AWS_PROFILE , else default . Access keys in the profile, a credential_process , single sign-on and assumed roles all work. Single sign-on and assumed roles are resolved through the AWS CLI, which must be installed; run aws sso login --profile my-profile first. The region comes from the provider's region setting, then AWS_REGION or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION , then the profile's own region, and is us-east-1 if none of those is set. Set it explicitly if your models are enabled elsewhere. base_url in the table, if you set it, replaces the address requests to run a model are sent to ( https://bedrock-runtime.<region>.amazonaws.com ). Things to know: Model names. The list offers the models your account can call in that region. Most current models are off

How full the model's context is, shown at the top of the agent panel, and when a long conversation is compacted (see Long conversations ) both depend on how much the model accepts. Astrum finds that out as follows, using the first that applies: A context_window you set in the config file: [models."my-local-model"] context_window = 32000 Name the table "provider/model" , as in [models."work/my-model"] , to cover one provider only. What the provider reports, asked once per model when you first use it: Anthropic describes each model's input limit, and Ollama running on the same machine lists it for the models it forwards to a hosted service. Otherwise an assumption: 128,000 tokens for OpenAI-compatible models, and 200,000 for Anthropic and Amazon Bedrock. A model that Ollama runs on your own machine falls under 3 even though Ollama reports a size for it, because Ollama serves a local model with the context it was set up to give it, which can be much less than the model's maximum. Set context_window for those. A figure that is too low only means compacting earlier than necessary; one that is too high means the conversation will not be compacted in time by itself. /usage shows the figure in use.

max_tokens under [agent] limits how many tokens one reply may have: [agent] max_tokens = 16000 Unset, Astrum asks Anthropic for up to 32,000 tokens and leaves the limit to the provider elsewhere. A reply cut off at the limit stops the turn, with a message saying so: raise max_tokens , or ask for a shorter answer.

Standing instructions for the agent go in plain Markdown files named AGENTS.md : ~/.config/astrum/AGENTS.md holds your own rules, for every project: how you like things done, tools you prefer, things never to touch. An AGENTS.md in a project holds that project's rules: how to build and test it, its conventions. Astrum reads the one in the shell's current directory and those in the directories above it, up to the top of the repository (the directory holding .git ) or your home directory, whichever comes first. Outside your home directory, with no repository, only the one in the current directory is read: a directory such as /tmp is anyone's. One that is a link to a file outside the project (outside the repository, or outside its own directory where there is none) is not read, so a project cannot put a file of yours, such as ~/.netrc , before the model. A rules file is whatever you would tell someone new to the work. For example: # Working on this project - Build with `make` and test with `make test`; run the tests before saying a change is done. - Never change anything under `vendor/`. - Write commit messages in the present tense. Short, specific rules work best.

The files are read at the start of every turn, so an edit applies from your next message. The agent panel says which files it is following ("Following the rules in ~/.config/astrum/AGENTS.md and AGENTS.md ."), and says it again when that changes. They are given to the agent in order: your own file first, then the project's, from the one furthest up down to the one in the current directory. When rules disagree, the file closest to the current directory wins, and what you ask for in the conversation wins over all of them. Each file is limited to 32 KB. What is beyond that is left out, and the agent is told so. An empty file is passed over. Up to six of a project's files are read, the closest ones. Rules are not part of the conversation: compacting a long conversation leaves them as they are. In a tab on another machine, an AGENTS.md in the project there is read along with your own from this machine (see Other machines ).

A line or two for the agent can also go in the config file, under [agent] : [agent] instructions = "Prefer ripgrep over grep." It is added to what the agent is told in every tab and every project, ahead of the rules files, and applies from the next message once the file is saved. Anything longer is easier to keep in ~/.config/astrum/AGENTS.md .

A skill is instructions for a particular kind of work, kept in a folder of its own with whatever it needs: scripts, templates, reference files. It is the layout other agents use, so a skill written for one of them works here as it is. release-notes/ SKILL.md scripts/changes.sh The agent is shown only each skill's name and description, so having many skills costs little. When one fits what you ask, it loads the rest and follows it.

SKILL.md begins with a short front matter, then the instructions: --- name: release-notes description: Write release notes for recent commits. Use when asked for release notes. --- 1. Run `scripts/changes.sh N` from this skill's folder ... name is what the agent and the slash menu know the skill by: letters, digits, - , _ and . , up to 64 of them, not starting with - or . . Without one, or with one that cannot be used, the folder's name is used. description says what the skill is for and when it is of use. It is all the agent sees of the skill until it loads it, so say when to use it. Without one, the first line of the instructions stands in. Up to 1,024 characters are used. Other keys in the front matter, such as license and metadata , are passed over. The instructions are read up to 64 KB. SKILL.md must be a file in the skill's folder: one that is a link to a file outside it is passed over (the whole folder can be a link). The other files in the folder (down to four levels, up to 200 of them, hidden ones left out) are listed for the agent when it loads the skill. It can read any of them, up to 256 KB each, and nothing outside the folder.

Each of these is a folder of skill folders: ~/.config/astrum/skills/ : yours, for every project. Folders you list as skill_dirs under [agent] : [agent] skill_dirs = ["~/shared-skills"] # a relative path starts from your home folder A project's .agents/skills/ or .astrum/skills/ , in the shell's current directory and the directories above it, as far up as for AGENTS.md : to the top of the repository or your home directory, whichever comes first (outside your home directory, with no repository, the current directory's only). Where two skills have the same name, the later in that list wins: a project's over one from skill_dirs , and that over your own; among a project's folders, the closest. Skills are looked for afresh at the start of every turn, so a skill you add is there from your next message. Up to 100 are offered from each of the three, so a project with a great many does not leave out your own.

When a skill fits what you ask, the agent loads it before it starts (the panel shows Read the skill release-notes ) and follows it. It can read the skill's other files the same way. Loading a skill is never asked about: it only reads. A script a skill brings is run as any command is, in your shell, after the usual question, so a skill does not change what needs your approval.

To use one on purpose, type its name as a command in the panel, with what you want after it: /release-notes for 0.6.0 The slash menu offers the skills as you type, after Astrum's own commands, each with skill: , where it is from (yours, from skill_dirs , or this project) and its description. With nothing after the name, the agent does what the skill is for, here. A skill that has the name of one of Astrum's own commands ( /model , /help and the like) can still be loaded by the agent, but not chosen this way.

/skills lists the skills there are: each one's name, where it is from (yours, from skill_dirs , or this project), whether it is off, what it is for and its folder. A skill as a file, and the skills there are, from /skills To turn one off, choose ≡ menu → Settings → Skills (the row says how many there are, and how many are off), then choose the skill; choosing it again turns it back on. In the panel, /skills off name and /skills on name do the same. A skill that is off is not shown to the agent, and /name says it is off. The choice is remembered, for every session.

In a tab on another machine, or with the agent taken into an ssh , the agent is offered your own skills, which stay on your machine. A project's skills are read only when the project is on this machine. A script one of your skills brings is put on the other machine by Astrum when the agent asks for it, in ~/.cache/astrum/skills/ there, as it is; one larger than 256 KB is not put there. In an ssh with nothing of Astrum's on the other side, the agent reads the script and writes it there itself, with a command you approve. See Other machines .

h: What a server gives the agent
x: An MCP server gives the agent tools of its own: a program on your machine (one that reads your project's issues, searches documentation, queries a database), or a service on the network. MCP, the Model Context Protocol , is a common way for programs to offer tools to an agent, and many servers are already written. Their tools are offered beside the agent's own. The agent uses one when it fits what you ask, and the panel shows each use as Used search_issues (github) with what it was given. Before a tool is used you are asked, as you are before a command runs, unless you have allowed it. Astrum uses a server's tools and nothing else of what the protocol has: it does not read a server's prompts or resources, and offers servers nothing in return (no sampling, no roots, no questions put to you). Each server is a table of its own under [mcp] in the config file. Its name is what /mcp calls it, and the start of the names the agent knows its tools by ( github__search_issues ): letters, digits, - and _ , up to 32 of them. A table that cannot be used as it is written (one with both command and url , or with neither) is reported as a problem with the config file.

[mcp.files] command = "npx" args = ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/Users/me/projects"] allow = ["read_*", "list_*", "search_*"] # used without asking command is the program and args its arguments; Astrum talks to it over its standard input and output. A program fetched on its first run, as npx and uvx do, may take a while, so a server is given a minute to answer when it starts. The program runs in a process group and an environment of its own. It gets what finding and running things needs ( PATH , HOME , USER , SHELL , TERM , the language and time-zone settings, the XDG_ folders, and the certificate and proxy settings) and what you give it in env . It does not get your API keys, or anything else from your environment. It runs in your home folder unless cwd says otherwise: [mcp.mine] command = "my-server" # a server of your own, as an example env = { MY_SERVER_DATA = "${HOME}/data" } cwd = "${HOME}/work" ${NAME} in command , args , env , cwd and headers stands for that variable as the session's server has it, which is the environment the session was started with. What a program writes to its error output is kept: /mcp log name shows the last 40 lines of it. A token for a program [mcp.github] command = "github-mcp-server" args = ["stdio"] token_env = "GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN" # given the token from /mcp key github tools = ["get_*", "list_*", "search_*"] # only these are offered /mcp key github in the panel asks for the token, shows it as dots while you

[mcp.docs] url = "https://mcp.example.com/mcp" A server on the network is reached over https:// . http:// is accepted only for one on this machine ( localhost , 127.0.0.1 ), so that what is sent to a server elsewhere (a token, your data) cannot be read on the way. headers adds headers to every request, with ${NAME} as for env . A redirect from the server is not followed: what goes with a request (the headers, a token) goes to the address in url and no other. /mcp shows where the server tried to send Astrum; if that is where it is, give that address as its url . A token If the server wants a token, /mcp key docs asks for one and keeps it in the password store. It is sent with every request, as Authorization: Bearer . The token is kept with the address it was given for. If the entry's url is changed, the token is not sent to the new address, and /mcp says so: store it again with /mcp key docs . The same goes for a sign-in. Signing in If the server asks you to sign in, Astrum says so when it starts the server, and /mcp shows it. To sign in, choose ≡ menu → Settings → MCP servers and then the server, or type /mcp signin docs in the panel. Your browser opens at the server's sign-in page (OAuth). Astrum registers itself with the service where the service lets it. Where it does not, give the client id the service gave you as client_id , and the scope to ask for as scope if it needs one. h: Which tools, and which without asking
x: tools and allow take tool names, where * stands for anything: tools limits which of a server's tools are offered to the agent at all. Without it, all of them are, up to 500 from one server. allow lists the tools that may be used without asking. Without it, every use is asked about. /mcp tools name lists a server's tools, and says which are not offered (not in tools ) and which are used without asking. What a server says of its own tools (that one only reads, say) is not taken on trust: it is your allow that counts.

Before a tool is used you are asked, as you are before a command runs: "Use search_issues from github?", with its arguments in full. Click a choice or press its letter: Yes ( y ): the tool is used, this once. Yes, don't ask again this session ( a ): the tool is used, and this tab's agent stops asking for anything, commands included, as on autopilot until the session ends. To let particular tools through without that, list them in allow instead. No, do something else ( n ): the tool is not used. Type what the agent should do instead, or press Esc to just decline. On autopilot no tool is asked about. See Approvals and How much it does on its own . A tool that is not in allow is asked about, with what it would be given

The servers are started the first time the agent is asked something (or when /mcp or the settings look at them), not when Astrum starts, and they run for as long as the session does. The first question waits up to 20 seconds for servers that are still starting, and the panel says "Starting MCP servers" meanwhile. A server that stops after it has been running a while is started again by itself, up to three times. After that, or if it stops soon after starting, its status says why. Once the servers are in use, saving the config file starts a server again if its entry changed, starts one you added, and ends one you took out. The servers are the session's: every tab's agent uses the same ones. When the session ends, so do they; a program is ended together with everything it started. timeout sets how many seconds one use of a tool may take, 120 unless set. enabled = false keeps a server off.

Choose ≡ menu → Settings → MCP servers . The row says how many servers are ready, starting, off or in need of a look, and choosing it lists them, each with how it is doing. Choosing a server there turns it off for this session, or on again, or signs in to one that asks. In the panel, /mcp says the same at more length: for each server, whether it is not started yet, starting, ready (with how many of its tools are offered, and the name and version it gives), failed and why, asking to be signed in to, or off. The commands below do the rest. An answer made with an MCP server's tool, and what /mcp says of the servers Command What it does /mcp Every server and how it is doing. /mcp tools name The server's tools: which are offered, and which are used without asking. /mcp log name What the program last wrote to its error output. /mcp restart name Start the server again. /mcp restart alone starts every server again. /mcp off name Turn the server off for this session; its tools are no longer offered. /mcp on name Turn it on again. /mcp key name Store a token for it. /mcp key name remove forgets the token. /mcp signin name Sign in to it in your browser. /mcp paste address Finish a sign-in whose browser is on another machine. /mcp signout name Forget its sign-in.

The tools act on your own machine. The servers run where Astrum runs, whatever the tab. In a tab on another machine, or with the agent taken into an ssh , the agent is told that the servers are not where its shell is, and that what their tools read and change is on your own machine. What a tool returns is shown to the model as text, with the same hiding of secrets and the same clipping as a command's output. A picture or a recording is named, not passed on, and so is a file returned as data rather than as text. A tool's answer is that server's word. The agent is told to weigh it as it would a program's output, and not to act on instructions in it that you did not give. That is guidance for the model, not a guarantee. Tokens and sign-ins are kept in the system's password store, not in the config file, and are hidden from the model as your API keys are. A program you add runs as you , with your permissions. allow is for tools whose effects you are content not to see first.

Each tab has an agent of its own, with its own conversation, and they work at the same time: one can run the tests in one tab while you ask another about something else. Ask, go to another tab, and carry on. You need not keep checking on them: the tab bar and the status bar say how each is doing, one list shows them all, and your terminal is told when one needs you. Within its tab, an agent works in the pane the keyboard was in when you asked, and stays there until it has finished (see The agent ).

A mark before a tab's name says how its agent is doing: Mark What it means a spinner The tab's agent is at work. ? The agent is asking you something. ✓ The agent finished while you were in another tab. ✗ The agent stopped with an error while you were in another tab. ✓ and ✗ stay until you look at the tab. Other news is marked with ● : a command that finished, or a bell, in a tab you have not looked at since; a ● in another color says that a command is still running there.

When agents in other tabs are asking or at work, the status bar says how many: ? 1 agent asking , or a spinner and 2 agents working . While any agent is asking, those are the ones it counts. Click it to see them all.

One list shows every tab's agent. To open it: click the count on the status bar ( ? 1 agent asking , 2 agents working ); choose ≡ menu → Every agent at a glance; press Ctrl+B A (a capital A); type /agents in the agent panel. Every tab's agent in one list Each tab has a row: its number and name, what its agent is doing, and on a second line what it is on, its model and the tokens its conversation has used. A ● marks news you have not seen. The row says What it means asks: Run this command? It is waiting for your answer. The second line has the command, or the start of what it would change. Running command for 1m 20s It is at work, and has been for that long. The second line has the command or the tool it is on. following a command it started A command it started is still running after the agent stopped waiting for it. finished 3m 2s ago It is done. stopped 40s ago It ended with an error, which the second line gives. stopped by you 5s ago You stopped it. ready There is a conversation, and nothing is going on. no conversation Nothing has been asked in that tab yet. Click a row, or its Open button, to go to that tab's agent: the tab comes to the front with the agent panel open and the keyboard in it. With the keyboard, Up and Down choose a row, Enter goes to it, and Esc closes the list. When the list opens, the row already chosen is the first agent that is asking, else the first with news, else the tab in front.

The row of an agent that asks to run a command has a Yes button when the list can show you the whole command: one line, short enough to fit, with no warning attached. Click it, or choose the row and press y , to answer yes without leaving where you are. It is the same as Yes on the question itself: the command runs. Everything else is answered in its tab: a command of several lines or too long to show, one that comes with a warning, a change to a file, an MCP tool, and any answer but yes (editing the command first, or declining). For those the row has only Open . A question that has only just appeared takes no yes from the list for a moment, so a click meant for the one before it is not taken as an answer.

h: Being told when an agent needs you
x: When an agent in a tab you are not looking at asks something, finishes, or stops with an error, your terminal is told: with a notification such as "Astrum: The agent in tab 2 (tests) is asking you something" where the terminal is known to show one, and with the bell otherwise: Terminal How it is told iTerm2, WezTerm, Ghostty A notification, sent as OSC 9. kitty A notification, sent as OSC 99. foot A notification, sent as OSC 777. any other, or astrum run inside a terminal multiplexer The bell. Astrum recognizes the terminal from the environment astrum is started in ( TERM_PROGRAM , TERM and the like). Where that does not say, as can happen over SSH, or to choose another way, set ASTRUM_NOTIFY before starting astrum : ASTRUM_NOTIFY=osc777 astrum osc9 , osc99 and osc777 choose that kind of notification, and none the bell alone. Each terminal window attached to the session is told on its own, in its own way, and a window that has that tab in front is not told at all. Whether a notification then appears on screen is up to the terminal and the system's notification settings.

The model. One model is chosen for the session: choosing another in one tab changes it for every tab's agent from its next request. See Providers and models . The autonomy level is the session's too. A Yes, don't ask again this session given to one tab's agent applies to that tab alone. See How much it does on its own . MCP servers are the session's, and every tab's agent uses the same ones. See MCP servers . Rules and skills come from the files of each tab's own directory, with your own beside them. See Rules and skills . Conversations are each tab's own, and are saved one by one. /conversations lists them all, with the tab each one is open in; a conversation can be open in one tab at a time. See Conversations .

Astrum's settings are in one file, config.toml . To see where it is: astrum config It is ~/.config/astrum/config.toml , or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/astrum/config.toml when XDG_CONFIG_HOME is set. ASTRUM_CONFIG_DIR names another folder for it altogether. If there is no file yet, the command says so. To write a commented starter file there: astrum config --init --init leaves a file that is already there alone. In the agent panel, /config also says where the file is, and writes the starter file if there is none. Every setting is optional. One that is not in the file has its default, so the file needs only the lines you want to change. The file is TOML: the settings at the top level come before the first line in square brackets, because a line written below [agent] belongs to [agent] . The whole starter file is at the end of this page .

h: Changes take effect when you save
x: A running session reads the file again as soon as it is saved, and says Settings reloaded from the config file . Nothing needs restarting, with three exceptions: scrollback and shell apply to shells started afterwards. truecolor applies to terminals that attach afterwards: detach ( ≡ menu → Detach) and run astrum again. A key held in an environment variable reaches a running session with astrum reload , run in the shell that has it. See Providers and models . If the file cannot be used as it is (a missing quote, a value that is not one of the choices, an MCP server written wrongly), Astrum says Config problem, nothing was changed with the reason, and the session carries on with what it had. A session that starts with a file it cannot read uses the defaults in place of everything the file says, and says Config problem with the reason. A smaller problem, such as a color that is not a color or a key that is not a key, leaves the rest of the file to take effect and is reported as Settings reloaded. Config problem: and what it is. A setting whose name Astrum does not know is passed over without a word, so a misspelled one, or one written under the wrong table, has no effect at all. astrum keys prints what is wrong with the file as a whole and with its [keys] , after its list of keys; astrum themes does the same for a theme of your own.

What you choose inside Astrum, on the settings screen, with /model and /theme , or by stepping through the autonomy levels, is written to state.toml , next to the config file. Astrum never rewrites config.toml itself. A choice in state.toml takes the place of the config file's value for that one setting. So once you have chosen a theme with /theme , changing theme in the config file makes no difference until that choice is forgotten. Forget the choices made here , the last row of the settings screen, empties state.toml (apart from the walkthrough having been seen) and hands every setting back to the config file. What state.toml can hold: the theme and theme_light , theme_terminal , agent_panel , copy_on_select , restore , the model and its provider, the autonomy level, ask_prefix , natural_language , redact_secrets , auto_compact , save_conversations , the skills you have turned off, and whether the walkthrough has been seen. Autopilot is never written down. Chosen inside Astrum, it lasts until the session ends. A session starts on autopilot only when the config file says autonomy = "auto" . Every session shares the file. A choice made in one session is kept when another writes the file, unless the other has made its own choice of that setting. A model needs its provider. A model chosen inside Astrum is used only while its provider is still built in or in the config file.

Every key Astrum uses can be changed in a [keys] table. A plain key is pressed after the prefix. A key with ctrl or alt works by itself, with no prefix, and is then Astrum's everywhere: programs no longer receive it. Naming an action replaces all of its keys, a list gives it several, and "none" leaves it without one. A key given to one action is taken from whatever had it before. [keys] new_tab = ["c", "ctrl+t"] # Ctrl+B c as before, and Ctrl+T directly next_tab = "alt+right" prev_tab = "alt+left" split_right = "v" detach_all = "none" The prefix key itself and the key that switches between the shell and the agent are not in the table: they are prefix and agent_key , at the top of the file. To see every action with the keys it has now: astrum keys The hint line, the menu and the help screen show the keys as you have set them. Every action and its default keys are in Mouse and keys .

A theme of your own is a [themes.<name>] table. Every color in it is optional: what you leave out comes from the theme named in based_on , or from Astrum Night if you name none. It then appears in /theme with the built-in ones. theme = "mine" [themes.mine] label = "Mine" based_on = "matrix" bg = "#000000" text = "#33ff66" accent = "#33ff66" Which colors there are, and what each one paints, is in A theme of your own on the Themes page.

Four providers are built in: ollama , openai , anthropic and bedrock . Any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint, such as a model server on your own machine or a company gateway, is a [providers.<name>] table. To make one of its models the default for every session, name both under [agent] : [agent] provider = "work" model = "my-model" [providers.work] kind = "openai" base_url = "https://llm.example.com/v1" api_key_env = "WORK_LLM_KEY" models = ["my-model"] Key What it is kind openai for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, anthropic , or bedrock . It must be given. base_url Where the endpoint is. Unless given, https://api.openai.com/v1 for openai and https://api.anthropic.com for anthropic . api_key_env The environment variable that holds the key. api_key The key itself, written in the file. A key here is used before one stored with /key and before the variable. models Models to offer in /model besides those the endpoint lists. region Amazon Bedrock: the AWS region. profile Amazon Bedrock: a profile from ~/.aws/credentials or ~/.aws/config . A table named after a built-in provider takes its place whole: nothing you leave out is taken from the built-in one, so give it every key it needs. A [providers.ollama] without base_url , for instance, would point at OpenAI's address. A [models."<id>"] table says how much context a model accepts, which Astrum otherwise asks the provider for or assumes. Name it "provider/model" to cover one provider only. [models."my-local-model"] context_window =
