Out of the box Astrum uses the theme called terminal : your terminal app's own colors, for the tab bar, the status bar and the agent panel, and for everything programs draw. So starting Astrum changes nothing about how your terminal looks, and if you change your terminal's color scheme, Astrum changes with it. Its highlights are your terminal's own standard colors, and a chosen row is shown in reverse. In the list of themes it is called Terminal (follow host colors) .

Open the list of themes with ≡ menu → Choose a theme, or from ≡ menu → Settings → Theme. From the keyboard, press Ctrl+B then s , or type /theme in the agent panel. The list is a live preview. The theme you are on is put on the whole screen at once, the session behind the list included, so you see it on your own work before you choose it. Turn the mouse wheel over the list, or press the arrow keys ↑ and ↓ , to move from theme to theme. Click a theme, or press Enter , to keep it. Click outside the list, or press Esc , to go back to the theme you had. Type to narrow the list to the themes whose names hold what you typed. Moving through the list puts each theme on the screen To choose one by name, give it to /theme : /theme nord . Capitals do not matter and spaces count as dashes, so /theme Blade Runner 2049 works too. A theme chosen inside Astrum is remembered for every session, in state.toml . To set it in the config file instead, put theme at the top of the file: theme = "nord" A theme chosen inside Astrum takes the place of the config file's until it is forgotten: see Choices made inside Astrum . astrum themes lists the name of every theme there is, yours included.

A chosen theme colors Astrum's own bars and panel, and with them what programs draw: their sixteen standard colors, and the plain text and background, are taken from the theme. So a theme is one look, rather than Astrum's bars in one set of colors around a shell in another. A program that asks the terminal for its colors, to tell a dark screen from a light one, is told the theme's. Colors a program gives exactly, as 24-bit colors or from the 256-color palette beyond its first sixteen, are drawn as the program gave them. To keep a theme to Astrum's bars and panel and leave programs in your terminal's own colors, turn off Programs use the theme's colors too on the settings screen, or set: theme_terminal = false With the terminal theme this makes no difference: there is nothing to recolor programs with.

h: A light theme for a light terminal
x: A terminal that is light by day and dark by night can have a theme for each. theme is the one for a dark background and theme_light the one for a light background: theme = "tokyo-night" theme_light = "catppuccin-latte" Which of the two applies is read from the terminal each time one attaches: Astrum asks it what color its background is. A terminal that does not answer counts as dark. While theme_light is set, a theme chosen in /theme goes to whichever the terminal is now, so one chosen on a light background becomes the light theme. With the default terminal theme there is nothing to set: it is your terminal's own colors either way. Among the built-in themes, Catppuccin Latte is the light one.

A terminal that supports 24-bit color is sent each theme's exact colors. Others are sent the nearest match from the 256-color palette. Astrum tells which a terminal is from what it says about itself ( COLORTERM , TERM and TERM_PROGRAM ), each time one attaches. Over SSH, where terminals often cannot say that they have 24-bit color, colors can look reduced. Then set: truecolor = true If a terminal claims 24-bit color and shows it wrongly, truecolor = false sends it the 256-color palette instead. Either applies to terminals that attach after it is set: detach and run astrum again. Programs inside Astrum are always told that 24-bit color is there ( COLORTERM=truecolor ), and Astrum turns what it draws into what your terminal can show.

A theme of your own is a table in the config file. Every color in it is optional: what you leave out comes from the theme named in based_on . It then appears in /theme and astrum themes with the built-in ones, and is used like them. theme = "mine" [themes.mine] label = "Mine" based_on = "matrix" bg = "#000000" text = "#33ff66" accent = "#33ff66" The name is the table's: [themes.mine] is mine . It can have letters, digits and dashes; capitals are taken as small letters, and spaces and underscores as dashes. label is what the list of themes shows. Without one, it shows the name. based_on names the theme to start from: any built-in one except terminal , or another of your own. Without it, the theme starts from Astrum Night ( astrum ). A name that is not a theme starts it from Astrum Night as well, with a note saying so. Colors are written "#rrggbb" , or in short as "#rgb" . A theme of yours with a built-in theme's name takes the built-in one's place in the list. To change a few colors of a built-in theme and keep it as well, give yours another name and base it on that one. Changes to the table take effect as soon as the file is saved, on the theme in use too. Something that cannot be read, such as a color that is not a color, is left as the theme it is based on had it, and Astrum says what was wrong; astrum themes prints the same. Astrum's commands, options, files and environment variables, as the manual page gives them. This is the manual page that man astrum shows and astrum man prints. The install script puts it where man finds it.
astrum - a persistent terminal with tabs, mouse support and a built-in AI agent
astrum [ -s SESSION ] [ COMMAND ]

astrum runs inside the terminal you already use. It shows your own shell with a tab bar above it and a status bar below, keeps your shells running in the background when the window is closed, and has an agent that works in the same shell you do. Run with no command, it attaches to the session, starting it first if it is not running. Everything on screen can be clicked; ≡ menu in the status bar lists every action with the key that does the same. The prefix key is Ctrl+B unless changed.

attach Attach to the session, starting it if needed. This is what happens when no command is given. ls List running sessions, and stopped ones whose tabs would come back. kill [ --all ] [ --forget ] Stop a session and close its shells. Its tabs come back the next time it is started, unless --forget is given. --all stops every session. config [ --init ] Show where the config file is. --init writes a commented starter file there. themes [ --json ] List the color themes, the built-in ones and your own; --json gives their colors as well. keys [ --json ] List what Astrum's keys do, with the keys each action has now; --json as JSON. reload Have a running session read its settings, providers and keys again, passing along the key variables of the shell it is run from. service install | uninstall | status Run the session under the system's service manager (launchd on macOS, the systemd user manager on Linux), so that it starts at login and is started again if it stops. install --print shows what would be written without doing it. completions bash | zsh | fish Print a completion script for that shell. man Print this manual page.
-s , --session NAME The session to act on. Each session has its own tabs. The default is default . -h , --help Show help. -V , --version Show the version.

Astrum reaches it with your own ssh (your keys, jump hosts and config as they are; its questions are shown in the pane), and its own program there keeps the shells. They and what runs in them outlast a dropped connection, a closed laptop and a restart of Astrum here; the pane picks up where it left off, or is shown the screen as it now stands. Such a tab is an ordinary one: splits open on the same machine, and scrollback, search, links and pictures work. The tab and the status bar say which machine it is on. The agent works there with all its tools. Commands run in the shell there; reading, searching and changing files (with the diff to approve first) are carried out there. The model and your keys stay here. If Astrum is not on the machine, it asks, then copies the release build for it over the SSH connection into ~/.local/bin , with the checksum verified on your machine first. No root, no package manager, and the machine needs no internet access. download_base names a mirror or a folder to take the build from. The two sides may be different versions as long as they speak the same link language (a number of its own, now 1). An older Astrum there is replaced only when you say so; a newer one never. Agent depth: conversations that last, ways to ask without leaving the shell, and more tools with more safeguards around them. Conversations and context Conversations are saved as they happen and survive the session ending. /resume reopens the most recent one from the current directory (or from anywhere, if there is none); /conversations lists them all, to reopen or delete. Conversations unused for 90 days are deleted ( keep_conversations_days ); save_conversations = false turns saving off. /compact replaces the conversation so far with a summary the agent continues from. It happens by itself when the model's context is nearly full or the conversation reaches 200,000 tokens, mid-task included, and when a provider refuses a request as too long. auto_compact and compact_limit control it. Rules files: the agent follows ~/.config/astrum/AGENTS.md and the AGENTS.md files of the project you are in, and says which ones apply. The agent panel shows how full the context is and the conversation's tokens: in, cached, out and total. /usage breaks it down. A model's context size is taken from the provider where it reports one (Anthropic, and Ollama's hosted models), and a [models."id"] table in the config file sets it for any model. The first release: a persistent terminal with tabs, mouse support and a built-in agent, as one self-contained binary. Sessions and tabs A background server per session keeps your shells running when the terminal window, or the whole terminal app, is closed. Run astrum again to return. Named sessions ( astrum -s work ), astrum ls , astrum kill . Tabs: create, switch, close and rename, from the keyboard ( Ctrl+B prefix) or with the mouse. New tabs open in the current directory. The same session can be open in several terminal windows; it takes the size of the one used most recently. Terminal Full terminal emulation with 10,000 lines of scrollback, so editors, pagers and other full-screen programs work as usual. Mouse: wheel scrollback; drag, double-click and triple-click selection that copies on release; mouse events pass through to programs that use them. Shell integration for zsh, bash and fish, loaded automatically, that tracks the working directory and where each command starts and ends. 24-bit color where the terminal supports it, with an automatic fallback to the 256-color palette where it does not. 14 color themes with live preview, including one that follows the terminal app's own colors. Agent Ctrl+Space switches between the shell and the agent. The agent's commands run in your live shell, where you can watch them and take over. Three autonomy levels: ask first (default), auto-run read-only commands, and autopilot. Destructive commands always ask. Approval prompts let
